Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette: Rohan, a 32-year-old South Asian man, had been working as a housekeeper for five years when his life took a drastic turn. One evening, while walking home from work, he was mugged by a group of teenagers in an alleyway near his apartment complex. The memory of that night remained etched in his mind like a fresh wound. When the memory returned, as it often did, Rohan felt physical pain in the same parts of his body where he had been kicked and punched during the assault. His memories of the event were vivid and detailed - the smell of garbage, the sound of laughter, and the feeling of helplessness. Rohan's wife, Priya, noticed a change in him after that night. He became increasingly withdrawn and started questioning everyone around him. "People are not what they seem," he would say to her, his eyes clouded with suspicion. Rohan couldn't shake off the feeling that anyone could be a potential threat, just like those teenagers who had attacked him for no reason. His mistrust extended beyond strangers; even friends and family members seemed untrustworthy in his eyes. As time passed, Rohan's memories of the mugging became more intertwined with his growing sense of paranoia. When he recalled the event, he couldn't help but think that it was a stark reminder of how the world is a truly dangerous place. His memories served as evidence to support his negative appraisals - proof that people were inherently untrustworthy and that the world was hostile. Rohan's occupation made things worse. As a housekeeper, he had to interact with new people every day, which only fueled his mistrust. He would often find himself wondering if the guests whose rooms he cleaned might be hiding something or plotting against him. These thoughts would lead him back to memories of that fateful night, and he would feel the same wave of pain wash over him. Priya tried to reassure Rohan, but her words seemed hollow in the face of his lived experience. His memories and negative appraisals had formed a vicious cycle, each reinforcing the other until it became hard for him to distinguish between reality and paranoia. The world outside felt like a battlefield, and Rohan felt constantly on edge, waiting for the next attack. It was when he started noticing changes in his work performance - missed deadlines, forgotten tasks, and strained relationships with colleagues - that Rohan realized he needed help. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was losing himself to these memories and negative appraisals. With a deep sense of desperation, he reached out for therapy, hoping to break free from this cycle of pain and mistrust. Rohan's current state is one of quiet despair. As he sits in his living room, surrounded by familiar comforts, he can't help but wonder if the world will ever feel safe again. What brings him hope is the possibility that therapy might help him rewire his thoughts, learn to trust others once more, and find a way to silence the echoes of that fateful night.
